newsitem.title: USA: Outgoing CBOE chief worried about new investors.
newsitem.headline: Outgoing CBOE chief worried about new investors.

text.p: Alger "Duke" Chapman, chairman of the Chicago Board Options Exchange (CBOE) who is to retire soon, said the most worrying thing about the market of late was the growing number of U.S. investors and brokers who have never really seen a down market.

"My biggest worry is that when when we have an economic downturn, usually six months in advance of that the market turns down and we have a whole generation of investors out there who have never seen a down market -- and brokers too," Chapman said in an interview with Reuters. He was in Tucson to attend a business conference on risk management.

"There are tens of thousands who have entered the business and millions who have bought stocks and mutual funds (in recent years)," he said. "I think it's a big burden on the industry to keep educating customers."

Generally, though, he added, there was not much to worry these days, even with the market at dizzying heights. He said investors had become much more sophisticated than in 1987, when he took over the helm at CBOE, the world's largest options exchange and soon saw the "Black Monday" stock market crash.
"I think the average investor today is more sophisticated than he was 10 years ago," Chapman said.

After the 1987 crash, trading volume in equity options plummetted and CBOE suffered big losses. But since then, volume has recovered pre-1987 levels, with CBOE exchange-wide volume totalling around 170-180 million contracts in each of the past three years. In 1996, CBOE volume totaled 174 million contracts, down about two percent from 1995, but trading in individual equity options rose 15 percent to a record 88.5 million contracts.

Industry executives attribute the remarkable comeback of interest in options to Chapman's efforts to educate the investor community. Educational courses run by CBOE's Optoins Institute, both for individual investors and professionals, have been packed in recent years and CBOE's website, http://www.cboe.com, receives some 700,000 hits a month.

"Under Duke's leadership, CBOE has undertaken a host of investor education initiatives," Arthur Levitt, chairman of the U.S. Securities and Exchange (SEC) said earlier at the Tucson conference. "CBOE has seen enormous growth during his tenure, including new records set last year for equity option trading volume."

"In an industry known for its creativity, Duke has earned a reputation as an innovator," Levitt, a high-school friend of Chapman, added. "He fostered the development of many new products, including long-term options known as LEAPS (long-term equity anticipation securities), FLEX options (exchange-traded options with negotiable terms), products based on foreign markets including options on ADRs (American depositary receipts) and sector and broad market index products."

While CBOE's S&P 100 index .OEX and S&P 500 .SPX options have always been the most actively traded equity index options in the world, recent years have seen rapid growth in LEAPS, technology sector index options and some ADR options such as those on Latin American phone companies.
Thomas Ascher, newly appointed CBOE vice chairman, told Reuters that order flows coming into the floor had become distinctively different from those in the late 1980s.
He noted that investors today would have a strategy to suit their needs before calling their brokers, whereas 10 years ago they would have just followed brokers' recommendations.
"I think it reflects their understanding of the products," he said.
Chapman is due to retire at the end of March, when he will be replaced by Bill Brodsky, currently president of the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME).

Brodsky told Reuters earlier in the week he felt little need to make any big changes to CBOE's business and that his goals were to build on Chapman's efforts in pursuing investor education and technological development.

During the last year towards the end of Chapman's reign, CBOE has acquired the options business at the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE), which Chapman expects to bring in at least about 12,000 to 13,000 contracts a day of current NYSE trade to CBOE, probably much more.
"I think there should be a natural growth from just being at CBOE," he said of the likely synergy effect when NYSE market makers start business in Chicago from April 28.
He said 1997 had already started at a record pace, with daily volume at about 770,000 contracts so far this month.
The strength of the market and the healthy position CBOE is in will help him retire with a peace of mind, Chapman said, adding that he will resign from all official capacities at CBOE.

"I feel strongly that the guy going out should not continue on the board." he said. He will continue to have part-time jobs on the board of several companies and organizations and intends to find a full-time job eventually.

"I'll also do something pretty much full time -- I have no idea what," he said. He added he was looking into something within the financial service sector but it was certain he wouldn't return to the legal business.
"Too many lawyers," he quipped.
